text: We introduce scalable deep kernels, which combine the structural properties of deep learning architectures with the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods. Specifically, we transform the inputs of a spectral mixture base kernel with a deep architecture, using local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and structure exploiting (Kronecker and Toeplitz) algebra for a scalable kernel representation. These closed-form kernels can be used as drop-in replacements for standard kernels, with benefits in expressive power and scalability. We jointly learn the properties of these kernels through the marginal likelihood of a Gaussian process. Inference and learning cost $O(n)$ for $n$ training points, and predictions cost $O(1)$ per test point. On a large and diverse collection of applications, including a dataset with 2 million examples, we show improved performance over scalable Gaussian processes with flexible kernel learning models, and stand-alone deep architectures.

text: Tree-structured recursive neural networks (TreeRNNs) for sentence meaning have been successful for many applications, but it remains an open question whether the fixed-length representations that they learn can support tasks as demanding as logical deduction. We pursue this question by evaluating whether two such models---plain TreeRNNs and tree-structured neural tensor networks (TreeRNTNs)---can correctly learn to identify logical relationships such as entailment and contradiction using these representations. In our first set of experiments, we generate artificial data from a logical grammar and use it to evaluate the models' ability to learn to handle basic relational reasoning, recursive structures, and quantification. We then evaluate the models on the more natural SICK challenge data. Both models perform competitively on the SICK data and generalize well in all three experiments on simulated data, suggesting that they can learn suitable representations for logical inference in natural language.

text: Understanding how ideas relate to each other is a fundamental question in many domains, ranging from intellectual history to public communication. Because ideas are naturally embedded in texts, we propose the first framework to systematically characterize the relations between ideas based on their occurrence in a corpus of documents, independent of how these ideas are represented. Combining two statistics --- cooccurrence within documents and prevalence correlation over time --- our approach reveals a number of different ways in which ideas can cooperate and compete. For instance, two ideas can closely track each other's prevalence over time, and yet rarely cooccur, almost like a "cold war" scenario. We observe that pairwise cooccurrence and prevalence correlation exhibit different distributions. We further demonstrate that our approach is able to uncover intriguing relations between ideas through in-depth case studies on news articles and research papers.

text: We introduce a novel framework for evaluating multimodal deep learning models with respect to their language understanding and generalization abilities. In this approach, artificial data is automatically generated according to the experimenter's specifications. The content of the data, both during training and evaluation, can be controlled in detail, which enables tasks to be created that require true generalization abilities, in particular the combination of previously introduced concepts in novel ways. We demonstrate the potential of our methodology by evaluating various visual question answering models on four different tasks, and show how our framework gives us detailed insights into their capabilities and limitations. By open-sourcing our framework, we hope to stimulate progress in the field of multimodal language understanding.

text: This paper presents our work on development of OWL-driven systems for formal representation and reasoning about terminological knowledge and facts in petrology. The long-term aim of our project is to provide solid foundations for a large-scale integration of various kinds of knowledge, including basic terms, rock classification algorithms, findings and reports. We describe three steps we have taken towards that goal here. First, we develop a semi-automated procedure for transforming a database of igneous rock samples to texts in a controlled natural language (CNL), and then a collection of OWL ontologies. Second, we create an OWL ontology of important petrology terms currently described in natural language thesauri. We describe a prototype of a tool for collecting definitions from domain experts. Third, we present an approach to formalization of current industrial standards for classification of rock samples, which requires linear equations in OWL 2. In conclusion, we discuss a range of opportunities arising from the use of semantic technologies in petrology and outline the future work in this area.

text: This works aims to design a statistical machine translation from English text to American Sign Language (ASL). The system is based on Moses tool with some modifications and the results are synthesized through a 3D avatar for interpretation. First, we translate the input text to gloss, a written form of ASL. text: In this paper we present the next step in our approach to neurobiologically plausible implementation of emotional reactions and behaviors for real-time autonomous robotic systems. text: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have shown promising performance for language modeling. However, traditional training of RNNs using back-propagation through time often suffers from overfitting. One reason for this is that stochastic optimization (used for large training sets) does not provide good estimates of model uncertainty. This paper leverages recent advances in stochastic gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo (also appropriate for large training sets) to learn weight uncertainty in RNNs. It yields a principled Bayesian learning algorithm, adding gradient noise during training (enhancing exploration of the model-parameter space) and model averaging when testing. Extensive experiments on various RNN models and across a broad range of applications demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach over stochastic optimization.

text: Controller synthesis for hybrid systems that satisfy temporal specifications expressing various system properties is a challenging problem that has drawn the attention of many researchers. However, making the assumption that such temporal properties are deterministic is far from the reality. For example, many of the properties the controller has to satisfy are learned through machine learning techniques based on sensor input data. In this paper, we propose a new logic, Probabilistic Signal Temporal Logic (PrSTL), as an expressive language to define the stochastic properties, and enforce probabilistic guarantees on them. We further show how to synthesize safe controllers using this logic for cyber-physical systems under the assumption that the stochastic properties are based on a set of Gaussian random variables. One of the key distinguishing features of PrSTL is that the encoded logic is adaptive and changes as the system encounters additional data and updates its beliefs about the latent random variables that define the safety properties. We demonstrate our approach by synthesizing safe controllers under the PrSTL specifications for multiple case studies including control of quadrotors and autonomous vehicles in dynamic environments.

text: Relational data sources are still one of the most popular ways to store enterprise or Web data, however, the issue with relational schema is the lack of a well-defined semantic description. A common ontology provides a way to represent the meaning of a relational schema and can facilitate the integration of heterogeneous data sources within a domain. Semantic labeling is achieved by mapping attributes from the data sources to the classes and properties in the ontology. We formulate this problem as a multi-class classification problem where previously labeled data sources are used to learn rules for labeling new data sources. The majority of existing approaches for semantic labeling have focused on data integration challenges such as naming conflicts and semantic heterogeneity. In addition, machine learning approaches typically have issues around class imbalance, lack of labeled instances and relative importance of attributes. To address these issues, we develop a new machine learning model with engineered features as well as two deep learning models which do not require extensive feature engineering. We evaluate our new approaches with the state-of-the-art.

text: We describe a seriation algorithm for ranking a set of items given pairwise comparisons between these items. Intuitively, the algorithm assigns similar rankings to items that compare similarly with all others. It does so by constructing a similarity matrix from pairwise comparisons, using seriation methods to reorder this matrix and construct a ranking. We first show that this spectral seriation algorithm recovers the true ranking when all pairwise comparisons are observed and consistent with a total order. We then show that ranking reconstruction is still exact when some pairwise comparisons are corrupted or missing, and that seriation based spectral ranking is more robust to noise than classical scoring methods. Finally, we bound the ranking error when only a random subset of the comparions are observed. An additional benefit of the seriation formulation is that it allows us to solve semi-supervised ranking problems. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that seriation based spectral ranking achieves competitive and in some cases superior performance compared to classical ranking methods.

text: In this article we introduce the operations of insertion and deletion working in a random-context and semi-conditional manner. We show that the conditional use of rules strictly increase the computational power. In the case of semi-conditional insertion-deletion systems context-free insertion and deletion rules of one symbol are sufficient to get the computational completeness. In the random context case our results expose an asymmetry between the computational power of insertion and deletion rules: systems of size $(2,0,0; 1,1,0)$ are computationally complete, while systems of size $(1,1,0;2,0,0)$ (and more generally of size $(1,1,0;p,1,1)$) are not. text: We present an end-to-end approach for automatically constructing task-oriented dialogue systems from minimal amounts of raw dialogue data. The method integrates an incremental semantic grammar framework—Dynamic Syntax and Type Theory with Records (DS-TTR)—with Reinforcement Learning (RL), treating language generation and dialogue management as a unified optimization problem. The resulting systems operate incrementally, processing dialogue at the word level, a property known to facilitate natural and spontaneous interactions. We posit that the expressive linguistic structure embedded in the grammar enables the system to handle a vast array of dialogue variations despite exposure to only a small training corpus. Our evaluation demonstrates that the model successfully processes 74% of the Facebook AI bAbI dataset when trained on merely 0.13% of available examples (5 dialogues). Furthermore, it handles 65% of bAbI+, a dataset we developed by systematically incorporating incremental dialogue phenomena including restarts and self-corrections into the original bAbI corpus. We provide a comparative analysis against MemN2N, a leading retrieval-based baseline, and demonstrate that MemN2N exhibits substantial performance degradation when encountering bAbI+ phenomena, even when trained on the complete bAbI dataset, whereas our approach maintains stronger semantic accuracy.

text: This document contains supplementary material for the paper "Multi-objective Reinforcement Learning with Continuous Pareto Frontier Approximation", published at the Twenty-Ninth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-15). The paper is about learning a continuous approximation of the Pareto frontier in Multi-Objective Markov Decision Problems (MOMDPs). We propose a policy-based approach that exploits gradient information to generate solutions close to the Pareto ones. Differently from previous policy-gradient multi-objective algorithms, where n optimization routines are use to have n solutions, our approach performs a single gradient-ascent run that at each step generates an improved continuous approximation of the Pareto frontier. The idea is to exploit a gradient-based approach to optimize the parameters of a function that defines a manifold in the policy parameter space so that the corresponding image in the objective space gets as close as possible to the Pareto frontier. Besides deriving how to compute and estimate such gradient, we will also discuss the non-trivial issue of defining a metric to assess the quality of the candidate Pareto frontiers. Finally, the properties of the proposed approach are empirically evaluated on two interesting MOMDPs.

text: This work introduces computational methods for inducing interpretable two-level Boolean classifiers expressed in either CNF (AND-of-ORs) or DNF (OR-of-ANDs) representations, with the objective of balancing predictive performance against model interpretability. Two distinct optimization frameworks are presented. The first employs an integer programming formulation that minimizes a composite objective combining classification errors and feature utilization, extending an existing LP relaxation technique from single-level to two-level rule structures. The second approach substitutes the standard 0-1 loss with Hamming distance, measuring deviation from the nearest rule achieving perfect classification on each instance. From this alternative formulation, block coordinate descent and alternating minimization procedures are derived. Empirical results demonstrate that two-level rules substantially outperform their single-level counterparts by exploiting significantly increased expressive capacity, with the Hamming distance-based algorithms consistently achieving superior results relative to competing two-level rule learning approaches. Additionally, a post-processing technique for converting fractional components in LP relaxation solutions to binary values demonstrates practical effectiveness.

text: Recent developments in neural variational inference have led to renewed interest in deep latent variable models. This work presents a unified variational inference framework applicable to both generative and conditional text models. Unlike conventional variational approaches that analytically approximate intractable posterior distributions over latent variables, our method employs an inference network that conditions on discrete text inputs to generate the variational distribution. We evaluate this framework across two distinct text modeling tasks: unsupervised document modeling and supervised question answering. Our neural document model integrates a continuous probabilistic document representation with a bag-of-words decoder, demonstrating superior performance on established benchmark corpora in terms of perplexity. The neural question answering model incorporates a stochastic representation layer integrated into an attention mechanism to capture the semantic relationship between question-answer pairs. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple question answering datasets, surpassing previously published performance metrics.

text: Argumentation consists of the exchange and assessment of interacting arguments, culminating in the selection of the most acceptable ones (e.g., to reach a decision or make a choice). Extending Dung’s 1995 framework, we aim to introduce “graduality” into the selection process, allowing the partition of arguments into more than the conventional two subsets of “selected” and “non‑selected” in order to capture varying degrees of acceptance. Our central intuition is that an argument becomes more acceptable when it can be preferred over its attackers. We first discuss the general principles that underlie a gradual valuation of arguments based on their interactions. Guided by these principles, we define several valuation models for abstract argumentation systems. Finally, we incorporate graduality into the notion of argument acceptability, proposing new acceptability classes and refining existing ones by exploiting the available gradual valuation.

text: Addressing the challenge of data sparsity remains a critical objective for collaborative filtering techniques. This study proposes a novel recommendation framework that leverages the inherent hierarchical organization of item spaces, grounded in the theory of Near Decomposability. By conceptualizing the item space as a Nearly Decomposable system, we identify clusters of highly interrelated elements and formalize their associated indirect proximity components. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of this decomposition, establishing sufficient conditions to ensure comprehensive item space coverage, even within cold-start constraints. Empirical evaluations conducted on the MovieLens and Yahoo!R2Music datasets demonstrate that our proposed model, NCDREC, aligns with theoretical expectations. Results across multiple performance metrics indicate that NCDREC significantly exceeds state-of-the-art baselines in terms of predictive accuracy, recommendation diversity, and robustness to data sparsity.

text: L1 regularisation has become a focal point of research on sparse learning, finding successful applications in fields ranging from signal acquisition and image coding to genomics and collaborative filtering. Although prior studies emphasise the many benefits of L1‑based approaches, we show that, in terms of predictive accuracy, L1 regularisation can fall far short of alternative sparsity‑inducing techniques. Concentrating on unsupervised latent‑variable models, we construct factor models that minimise an L1 penalty, Bayesian analogues of L1, and Bayesian factor models that impose a more stringent, L0‑like sparsity via spike‑and‑slab priors. The spike‑and‑slab Bayesian models promote sparsity while formally incorporating uncertainty and avoiding the excessive shrinkage of genuine non‑zero coefficients. Empirical evaluations on several data sets reveal that, even under comparable computational constraints, spike‑and‑slab Bayesian methods consistently surpass L1 minimisation in predictive performance. These findings call for a reassessment of the prevalent reliance on L1 regularisation in sparsity‑driven applications—particularly when generalisation to unseen data is paramount—and present a principled alternative that delivers superior generalisation across a wide range of conditions.

text: This study investigates the linguistic properties acquired by a reinforcement learning agent within the ActiveQA framework. ActiveQA conceptualizes question answering as a reinforcement learning problem, positioning an intermediary agent between the user and a closed-source question-answering system. The agent is tasked with optimizing answer quality by reformulating user queries into multiple variations via a sequence-to-sequence model and subsequently aggregating the retrieved results. This interaction represents a form of machine-to-machine communication, where the reformulation model must adapt its output to align with the underlying QA system’s processing characteristics. Our analysis reveals that the agent’s learned transformations do not correspond to human semantic intuitions; instead, the agent independently discovers established information retrieval strategies, including stemming and tf-idf re-weighting.

text: Decentralized control of cooperative systems describes a set of decision-makers pursuing a unified global objective. The challenge in obtaining optimal solutions arises when the agents do not have full visibility of the system’s global state during operation. The general formulation has been shown to be NEXP-complete. In this work, we identify families of decentralized control problems whose computational complexity lies between NEXP and P. In particular, we analyze problems characterized by independent state transitions, independent observations, and goal-driven objective functions. We demonstrate two algorithms that solve optimally useful subclasses of goal-oriented decentralized processes in polynomial time. The paper also investigates information exchange among the agents, which can enhance performance. We distinguish three modes of information sharing: indirect communication, direct communication, and the sharing of state features that are not controlled by the agents. Our findings indicate that, for each problem class considered, allowing direct or indirect communication does not alter the worst-case complexity. These results deepen the understanding of the complexity landscape of practical decentralized control problems and aid in the development of planning algorithms for such problems.

text: The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) is a recently proposed test statistic for two-sample test. Its quadratic time complexity, however, greatly hampers its availability to large-scale applications. To accelerate the MMD calculation, in this study we propose an efficient method called FastMMD. The core idea of FastMMD is to equivalently transform the MMD with shift-invariant kernels into the amplitude expectation of a linear combination of sinusoid components based on Bochner's theorem and Fourier transform (Rahimi & Recht, 2007). Taking advantage of sampling of Fourier transform, FastMMD decreases the time complexity for MMD calculation from $O(N^2 d)$ to $O(L N d)$, where $N$ and $d$ are the size and dimension of the sample set, respectively. Here $L$ is the number of basis functions for approximating kernels which determines the approximation accuracy. For kernels that are spherically invariant, the computation can be further accelerated to $O(L N \log d)$ by using the Fastfood technique (Le et al., 2013). The uniform convergence of our method has also been theoretically proved in both unbiased and biased estimates. We have further provided a geometric explanation for our method, namely ensemble of circular discrepancy, which facilitates us to understand the insight of MMD, and is hopeful to help arouse more extensive metrics for assessing two-sample test. Experimental results substantiate that FastMMD is with similar accuracy as exact MMD, while with faster computation speed and lower variance than the existing MMD approximation methods.

text: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) is a nature-inspired metaheuristic for solving continuous optimization problems. While the literature has exploited the notion of particle potential to establish convergence to local optima for slightly altered PSO schemes, here we show that, under particular conditions, the vanilla PSO—even with swarm-parameter settings that are reported to be effective—almost surely fails to converge to a local optimum. Consequently, these dimensions become irrelevant: their contributions to attractor updates become negligible and, with positive probability, never regain relevance. text: POMDPs are standard models for probabilistic planning problems, where an agent interacts with an uncertain environment. We study the problem of almost-sure reachability, where given a set of target states, the question is to decide whether there is a policy to ensure that the target set is reached with probability 1 (almost-surely). While in general the problem is EXPTIME-complete, in many practical cases policies with a small amount of memory suffice. Moreover, the existing solution to the problem is explicit, which first requires to construct explicitly an exponential reduction to a belief-support MDP. In this work, we first study the existence of observation-stationary strategies, which is NP-complete, and then small-memory strategies. We present a symbolic algorithm by an efficient encoding to SAT and using a SAT solver for the problem. We report experimental results demonstrating the scalability of our symbolic (SAT-based) approach.

text: In 1979 Stockman introduced the SSS* minimax search algorithm that domi- nates Alpha-Beta in the number of leaf nodes expanded. Further investigation of the algorithm showed that it had three serious drawbacks, which prevented its use by practitioners: it is difficult to understand, it has large memory requirements, and it is slow. This paper presents an alternate formulation of SSS*, in which it is implemented as a series of Alpha-Beta calls that use a transposition table (AB- SSS*). The reformulation solves all three perceived drawbacks of SSS*, making it a practical algorithm. Further, because the search is now based on Alpha-Beta, the extensive research on minimax search enhancements can be easily integrated into AB-SSS*. To test AB-SSS* in practise, it has been implemented in three state-of-the- art programs: for checkers, Othello and chess. AB-SSS* is comparable in performance to Alpha-Beta on leaf node count in all three games, making it a viable alternative to Alpha-Beta in practise. Whereas SSS* has usually been regarded as being entirely different from Alpha-Beta, it turns out to be just an Alpha-Beta enhancement, like null-window searching. This runs counter to published simulation results. Our research leads to the surprising result that iterative deepening versions of Alpha-Beta can expand fewer leaf nodes than iterative deepening versions of SSS* due to dynamic move re-ordering.

text: We present decentralized rollout sampling policy iteration (DecRSPI) - a new algorithm for multi-agent decision problems formalized as DEC-POMDPs. DecRSPI is designed to improve scalability and tackle problems that lack an explicit model. The algorithm uses Monte- Carlo methods to generate a sample of reachable belief states. Then it computes a joint policy for each belief state based on the rollout estimations. A new policy representation allows us to represent solutions compactly. The key benefits of the algorithm are its linear time complexity over the number of agents, its bounded memory usage and good solution quality. It can solve larger problems that are intractable for existing planning algorithms. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness and scalability of the approach.

text: We review the theory and practice of determining what parts of a data set are ultrametric. It is assumed that the data set, to begin with, is endowed with a metric, and we include discussion of how this can be brought about if a dissimilarity, only, holds. The basis for part of the metric-endowed data set being ultrametric is to consider triplets of the observables (vectors). We develop a novel consensus of hierarchical clusterings. We do this in order to have a framework (including visualization and supporting interpretation) for the parts of the data that are determined to be ultrametric. Furthermore a major objective is to determine locally ultrametric relationships as opposed to non-local ultrametric relationships. As part of this work, we also study a particular property of our ultrametricity coefficient, namely, it being a function of the difference of angles of the base angles of the isosceles triangle. This work is completed by a review of related work, on consensus hierarchies, and of a major new application, namely quantifying and interpreting the emotional content of narrative.

text: An ensemble inference mechanism is proposed on the Angry Birds domain. It is based on an efficient tree structure for encoding and representing game screenshots, where it exploits its enhanced modeling capability. This has the advantage to establish an informative feature space and modify the task of game playing to a regression analysis problem. To this direction, we assume that each type of object material and bird pair has its own Bayesian linear regression model. In this way, a multi-model regression framework is designed that simultaneously calculates the conditional expectations of several objects and makes a target decision through an ensemble of regression models. Learning procedure is performed according to an online estimation strategy for the model parameters. We provide comparative experimental results on several game levels that empirically illustrate the efficiency of the proposed methodology.

text: Poetry-writing in Sanskrit is riddled with problems for even those who know the language well. This is so because the rules that govern Sanskrit prosody are numerous and stringent. We propose a computational algorithm that converts prose given as E-text into poetry in accordance with the metrical rules of Sanskrit prosody, simultaneously taking care to ensure that sandhi or euphonic conjunction, which is compulsory in verse, is handled. The algorithm is considerably speeded up by a novel method of reducing the target search database. The algorithm further gives suggestions to the poet in case what he/she has given as the input prose is impossible to fit into any allowed metrical format. There is also an interactive component of the algorithm by which the algorithm interacts with the poet to resolve ambiguities. In addition, this unique work, which provides a solution to a problem that has never been addressed before, provides a simple yet effective speech recognition interface that would help the visually impaired dictate words in E-text, which is in turn versified by our Poetry Composer Engine.

text: Complex networks refer to large-scale graphs with nontrivial connection patterns. The salient and interesting features that the complex network study offer in comparison to graph theory are the emphasis on the dynamical properties of the networks and the ability of inherently uncovering pattern formation of the vertices. In this paper, we present a hybrid data classification technique combining a low level and a high level classifier. The low level term can be equipped with any traditional classification techniques, which realize the classification task considering only physical features (e.g., geometrical or statistical features) of the input data. On the other hand, the high level term has the ability of detecting data patterns with semantic meanings. In this way, the classification is realized by means of the extraction of the underlying network's features constructed from the input data. As a result, the high level classification process measures the compliance of the test instances with the pattern formation of the training data. Out of various high level perspectives that can be utilized to capture semantic meaning, we utilize the dynamical features that are generated from a tourist walker in a networked environment. Specifically, a weighted combination of transient and cycle lengths generated by the tourist walk is employed for that end. Interestingly, our study shows that the proposed technique is able to further improve the already optimized performance of traditional classification techniques.

text: In this paper, through multi-task ensemble framework we address three problems of emotion and sentiment analysis i.e. "emotion classification & intensity", "valence, arousal & dominance for emotion" and "valence & arousal} for sentiment". The underlying problems cover two granularities (i.e. coarse-grained and fine-grained) and a diverse range of domains (i.e. tweets, Facebook posts, news headlines, blogs, letters etc.). We obtain the performance improvement of 2-3 points on an average over single-task systems for most of the problems and domains.

text: The paper addresses the modular design of composite solving strategies for multicriteria ranking (sorting). Here a 'scale of creativity' that is close to creative levels proposed by Altshuller is used as the reference viewpoint: (i) a basic object, (ii) a selected object, (iii) a modified object, and (iv) a designed object (e.g., composition of object components). These levels maybe used in various parts of decision support systems (DSS) (e.g., information, operations, user). The paper focuses on the more creative above-mentioned level (i.e., composition or combinatorial synthesis) for the operational part (i.e., composite solving strategy). This is important for a search/exploration mode of decision making process with usage of various procedures and techniques and analysis/integration of obtained results. The paper describes methodological issues of decision technology and synthesis of composite strategy for multicriteria ranking. The synthesis of composite strategies is based on 'hierarchical morphological multicriteria design' (HMMD) which is based on selection and combination of design alternatives (DAs) (here: local procedures or techniques) while taking into account their quality and quality of their interconnections (IC). A new version of HMMD with interval multiset estimates for DAs is used. The operational environment of DSS COMBI for multicriteria ranking, consisting of a morphology of local procedures or techniques (as design alternatives DAs), is examined as a basic one.

text: Majority of the existing robot navigation systems, which facilitate the use of laser range finders, sonar sensors or artificial landmarks, has the ability to locate itself in an unknown environment and then build a map of the corresponding environment. Stereo vision, while still being a rapidly developing technique in the field of autonomous mobile robots, are currently less preferable due to its high implementation cost. text: Although deep learning models have proven effective at solving problems in natural language processing, the mechanism by which they come to their conclusions is often unclear. As a result, these models are generally treated as black boxes, yielding no insight of the underlying learned patterns. In this paper we consider Long Short Term Memory networks (LSTMs) and demonstrate a new approach for tracking the importance of a given input to the LSTM for a given output. By identifying consistently important patterns of words, we are able to distill state of the art LSTMs on sentiment analysis and question answering into a set of representative phrases. This representation is then quantitatively validated by using the extracted phrases to construct a simple, rule-based classifier which approximates the output of the LSTM.

text: In this paper, we address referring expression comprehension: localizing an image region described by a natural language expression. While most recent work treats expressions as a single unit, we propose to decompose them into three modular components related to subject appearance, location, and relationship to other objects. This allows us to flexibly adapt to expressions containing different types of information in an end-to-end framework. In our model, which we call the Modular Attention Network (MAttNet), two types of attention are utilized: language-based attention that learns the module weights as well as the word/phrase attention that each module should focus on; and visual attention that allows the subject and relationship modules to focus on relevant image components. Module weights combine scores from all three modules dynamically to output an overall score. Experiments show that MAttNet outperforms previous state-of-art methods by a large margin on both bounding-box-level and pixel-level comprehension tasks. Demo and code are provided.

text: We consider infinite-horizon stationary $γ$-discounted Markov Decision Processes, for which it is known that there exists a stationary optimal policy. Using Value and Policy Iteration with some error $ε$ at each iteration, it is well-known that one can compute stationary policies that are $\frac{2γ}{(1-γ)^2}ε$-optimal. After arguing that this guarantee is tight, we develop variations of Value and Policy Iteration for computing non-stationary policies that can be up to $\frac{2γ}{1-γ}ε$-optimal, which constitutes a significant improvement in the usual situation when $γ$ is close to 1. Surprisingly, this shows that the problem of "computing near-optimal non-stationary policies" is much simpler than that of "computing near-optimal stationary policies".

text: The field of Distributed Constraint Optimization Problems (DCOPs) has gained momentum, thanks to its suitability in capturing complex problems (e.g., multi-agent coordination and resource allocation problems) that are naturally distributed and cannot be realistically addressed in a centralized manner. The state of the art in solving DCOPs relies on the use of ad-hoc infrastructures and ad-hoc constraint solving procedures. This paper investigates an infrastructure for solving DCOPs that is completely built on logic programming technologies. In particular, the paper explores the use of a general constraint solver (a constraint logic programming system in this context) to handle the agent-level constraint solving. The preliminary experiments show that logic programming provides benefits over a state-of-the-art DCOP system, in terms of performance and scalability, opening the doors to the use of more advanced technology (e.g., search strategies and complex constraints) for solving DCOPs.

text: The idea of sensitivity in ant colony systems has been exploited in hybrid ant-based models with promising results for many combinatorial optimization problems. Heterogeneity is induced in the ant population by endowing individual ants with a certain level of sensitivity to the pheromone trail. The variable pheromone sensitivity within the same population of ants can potentially intensify the search while in the same time inducing diversity for the exploration of the environment. The performance of sensitive ant models is investigated for solving the generalized vehicle routing problem. Numerical results and comparisons are discussed and analysed with a focus on emphasizing any particular aspects and potential benefits related to hybrid ant-based models.

text: For some computational problems (e.g., product configuration, planning, diagnosis, query answering, phylogeny reconstruction) computing a set of similar/diverse solutions may be desirable for better decision-making. With this motivation, we studied several decision/optimization versions of this problem in the context of Answer Set Programming (ASP), analyzed their computational complexity, and introduced offline/online methods to compute similar/diverse solutions of such computational problems with respect to a given distance function. All these methods rely on the idea of computing solutions to a problem by means of finding the answer sets for an ASP program that describes the problem. The offline methods compute all solutions in advance using the ASP formulation of the problem with an ASP solver, like Clasp, and then identify similar/diverse solutions using clustering methods. The online methods compute similar/diverse solutions following one of the three approaches: by reformulating the ASP representation of the problem to compute similar/diverse solutions at once using an ASP solver; by computing similar/diverse solutions iteratively (one after other) using an ASP solver; by modifying the search algorithm of an ASP solver to compute similar/diverse solutions incrementally. We modified Clasp to implement the last online method and called it Clasp-NK. In the first two online methods, the given distance function is represented in ASP; in the last one it is implemented in C++. We showed the applicability and the effectiveness of these methods on reconstruction of similar/diverse phylogenies for Indo-European languages, and on several planning problems in Blocks World. We observed that in terms of computational efficiency the last online method outperforms the others; also it allows us to compute similar/diverse solutions when the distance function cannot be represented in ASP.

text: We present the sTeX+ system, a user-driven advancement of sTeX - a semantic extension of LaTeX that allows for producing high-quality PDF documents for (proof)reading and printing, as well as semantic XML/OMDoc documents for the Web or further processing. Originally sTeX had been created as an invasive, semantic frontend for authoring XML documents. Here, we used sTeX in a Software Engineering case study as a formalization tool. In order to deal with modular pre-semantic vocabularies and relations, we upgraded it to sTeX+ in a participatory design process. We present a tool chain that starts with an sTeX+ editor and ultimately serves the generated documents as XHTML+RDFa Linked Data via an OMDoc-enabled, versioned XML database. In the final output, all structural annotations are preserved in order to enable semantic information retrieval services.

text: We have previously reported a Bayesian algorithm for determining the coordinates of points in three-dimensional space from uncertain constraints.  This method is useful in the determination of biological molecular structure.  It is limited, however, by the requirement that the uncertainty in the constraints be normally distributed. In this paper, we present an extension of the original algorithm that allows constraint uncertainty to be represented as a mixture of Gaussians, and thereby allows arbitrary constraint distributions.  We illustrate the performance of this algorithm on a problem drawn from the domain of molecular structure determination, in which a multicomponent constraint representation produces a much more accurate solution than the old single component mechanism.  The new mechanism uses mixture distributions to decompose the problem into a set of independent problems with unimodal constraint uncertainty.  The results of the unimodal subproblems are periodically recombined using Bayes' law, to avoid combinatorial explosion.  The new algorithm is particularly suited for parallel implementation.

text: Consensus formation is investigated for multi-agent systems in which agents' beliefs are both vague and uncertain. Vagueness is represented by a third truth state meaning \emph{borderline}. This is combined with a probabilistic model of uncertainty. A belief combination operator is then proposed which exploits borderline truth values to enable agents with conflicting beliefs to reach a compromise. A number of simulation experiments are carried out in which agents apply this operator in pairwise interactions, under the bounded confidence restriction that the two agents' beliefs must be sufficiently consistent with each other before agreement can be reached. As well as studying the consensus operator in isolation we also investigate scenarios in which agents are influenced either directly or indirectly by the state of the world. For the former we conduct simulations which combine consensus formation with belief updating based on evidence. For the latter we investigate the effect of assuming that the closer an agent's beliefs are to the truth the more visible they are in the consensus building process. In all cases applying the consensus operators results in the population converging to a single shared belief which is both crisp and certain. Furthermore, simulations which combine consensus formation with evidential updating converge faster to a shared opinion which is closer to the actual state of the world than those in which beliefs are only changed as a result of directly receiving new evidence. Finally, if agent interactions are guided by belief quality measured as similarity to the true state of the world, then applying the consensus operator alone results in the population converging to a high quality shared belief.

text: The clique tree algorithm is the standard method for doing  inference in Bayesian networks. It works by manipulating clique potentials - distributions over the variables in a clique. While this approach works well for many networks, it is limited by the need to maintain an exact representation of the clique potentials. This paper presents a new unified approach that combines approximate inference and the clique tree algorithm, thereby circumventing this limitation. Many known approximate inference algorithms can be viewed as instances of this approach. The algorithm essentially does clique tree propagation, using approximate inference to estimate the densities in each clique. In many settings, the computation of the approximate clique potential can be done easily using statistical importance sampling. Iterations are used to gradually improve the quality of the estimation.

text: Text mining is becoming vital as Web 2.0 offers collaborative content creation and sharing. Now Researchers have growing interest in text mining methods for discovering knowledge. Text mining researchers come from variety of areas like: Natural Language Processing, Computational Linguistic, Machine Learning, and Statistics. Although there are various standard datasets available for traditional text mining tasks, but there are very few and expensive datasets for blog-mining task. Blogs, a new genre in web 2.0 is a digital diary of web user, which has chronological entries and contains a lot of useful knowledge, thus offers a lot of challenges and opportunities for text mining. In this paper, we report a new indigenous dataset for Pakistani Political Blogosphere. The paper describes the process of data collection, organization, and standardization. We have used this dataset for carrying out various text mining tasks for blogosphere, like: blog-search, political sentiments analysis and tracking, identification of influential blogger, and clustering of the blog-posts. We wish to offer this dataset free for others who aspire to pursue further in this domain.

text: GNU Prolog is a general-purpose implementation of the Prolog language, which distinguishes itself from most other systems by being, above all else, a native-code compiler which produces standalone executables which don't rely on any byte-code emulator or meta-interpreter. Other aspects which stand out include the explicit organization of the Prolog system as a multipass compiler, where intermediate representations are materialized, in Unix compiler tradition. GNU Prolog also includes an extensible and high-performance finite domain constraint solver, integrated with the Prolog language but implemented using independent lower-level mechanisms. This article discusses the main issues involved in designing and implementing GNU Prolog: requirements, system organization, performance and portability issues as well as its position with respect to other Prolog system implementations and the ISO standardization initiative.

text: Objective: Electronic health records contain extensive narrative content that offers valuable insights for medical research and data science applications. This study presents NILE (Narrative Information Linear Extraction), an open-source NLP tool designed specifically for processing and analyzing EHR text, which is made available to the medical informatics community. Methods: NILE employs a customized prefix-tree search mechanism for entity identification that recognizes shared prefixes and suffixes. Semantic interpretation is performed through rule-based finite state automata, enabling detection of negation, spatial context, modifiers, familial relationships, and irrelevant information. Results: NILE demonstrates processing speeds that exceed existing medical NLP systems by several orders of magnitude. Its performance in identifying clinical presence matches that of top-performing systems evaluated on the 2010 i2b2/VA NLP challenge benchmark. Conclusion: NILE represents a significant contribution to medical informatics and data science NLP applications, offering superior computational efficiency, competitive accuracy, and API accessibility for diverse implementation contexts.

text: Convolutional neural networks leverage textural and structural patterns in images as key features for image classification tasks. Preprocessing through image enhancement can augment image quality and subsequently boost CNN performance. Traditional image enhancement approaches, however, are optimized for human visual perception rather than machine learning objectives. This work proposes learning enhancement mechanisms specifically tailored to improve classification accuracy rather than perceptual quality. We introduce an integrated CNN framework that applies adaptive enhancement filters to extract task-specific image features through trainable end-to-end filter optimization. The proposed method is evaluated on four diverse benchmark datasets spanning fine-grained recognition, object detection, scene understanding, and texture analysis: CUB-200-2011, PASCAL-VOC2007, MIT-Indoor, and DTD. Results demonstrate consistent performance improvements across all tested datasets. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates generalizability by enhancing the classification performance of various standard CNN architectures.

text: In this paper we introduce the notion of Demand-Weighted Completeness, allowing estimation of the completeness of a knowledge base with respect to how it is used. Defining an entity by its classes, we employ usage data to predict the distribution over relations for that entity. For example, instances of person in a knowledge base may require a birth date, name and nationality to be considered complete. These predicted relation distributions enable detection of important gaps in the knowledge base, and define the required facts for unseen entities. Such characterisation of the knowledge base can also quantify how usage and completeness change over time. We demonstrate a method to measure Demand-Weighted Completeness, and show that a simple neural network model performs well at this prediction task.

text: Narrative structures pervade numerous forms of natural language text, reflecting the human tendency to frame experiences through storytelling. While there is widespread agreement that narrative comprehension necessitates the identification and monitoring of character motivations and their outcomes, computational approaches to this task remain underdeveloped. This work presents DesireDB, a novel annotated corpus containing expert-validated labels for desire expressions, supporting textual evidence for desire resolution, and categorical judgments regarding whether desires are satisfied based on narrative context. We conduct empirical evaluations of various computational techniques for desire fulfillment tracking and demonstrate that an LSTM Skip-Thought architecture achieves an F-measure of 0.7 on the dataset.

text: The proliferation of networked vehicle systems has expanded the potential attack vectors, posing risks not only to vehicle occupants but also to surrounding individuals. Such vulnerabilities stem from the reliance on the legacy CAN bus protocol, which provides minimal security infrastructure and lacks authentication mechanisms. Given that protocol replacement cannot address vulnerabilities in existing vehicles, we propose a data-driven approach utilizing machine learning to enhance automotive security. We implement a Hidden Markov Model capable of identifying anomalous operational states based on empirical vehicle data. During vehicle operation, this model enables real-time detection and alerting of security threats. The proposed solution is designed as a retrofit module compatible with both current and legacy vehicle architectures.

text: Large-scale multi-relational embedding refers to the task of learning the latent representations for entities and relations in large knowledge graphs. An effective and scalable solution for this problem is crucial for the true success of knowledge-based inference in a broad range of applications. This paper proposes a novel framework for optimizing the latent representations with respect to the \textit{analogical} properties of the embedded entities and relations. By formulating the learning objective in a differentiable fashion, our model enjoys both theoretical power and computational scalability, and significantly outperformed a large number of representative baseline methods on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the model offers an elegant unification of several well-known methods in multi-relational embedding, which can be proven to be special instantiations of our framework.

text: Recent advances in deep learning have revolutionized visual object detection, with neural networks achieving performance comparable to or exceeding human-level accuracy on certain standardized datasets. However, significant obstacles remain in the generalized detection of diverse concepts across arbitrary video content. This work presents an integrated framework that leverages neural network architectures, a comprehensive large-scale visual concept taxonomy, and an iterative active learning mechanism to enable rapid model adaptation for novel concept recognition. The paper describes the overall architecture of the proposed system, emphasizing the critical contribution of the ontological structure in directing concept acquisition, enhancing detection performance through improved recall, and enabling semantically-informed video retrieval capabilities for end users navigating annotated video collections.

text: Grapheme‑to‑phoneme conversion (g2p) is a prerequisite for both text‑to‑speech synthesis and automatic speech recognition. Existing g2p systems are typically monolingual, relying on language‑specific corpora or manually engineered rules, which hampers their applicability to low‑resource languages lacking such resources. To address this limitation, we propose a neural sequence‑to‑sequence model trained on spelling‑pronunciation pairs from hundreds of languages. The architecture employs a single shared encoder–decoder pair across all languages, thereby exploiting the inherent correspondences among diverse orthographies. Experiments demonstrate an 11 % reduction in phoneme error rate compared with methods that adapt high‑resource monolingual g2p models to low‑resource settings, while also yielding a considerably more compact model than prior approaches.

text: The Information Cascades Model characterizes the temporal dynamics of user activity on social networks. In this study we introduce a new framework for shaping such activity under the Continuous‑Time Information Cascades Model, enabling an administrator to exert localized control by allocating targeted resources that modify the diffusion process. The approach hinges on optimizing the spectral radius of the Hazard matrix—a metric known to govern the maximal influence attainable in a network—and benefits from a straightforward convex relaxation when the objective is to curtail cascade influence. We illustrate the versatility of the proposed activity‑shaping paradigm through scenarios such as quarantine and node immunization. Moreover, we propose the NetShape algorithm for influence minimization and demonstrate its superior performance relative to baseline and state‑of‑the‑art methods via simulations on real‑world social network data.

text: This study presents the inaugural application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to acquire policies for inquiry dialog systems (IDS). Experimental evaluations of (1) the DRL approach and (2) the proposed embedding framework demonstrate that their integration achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases surpassing, that of existing rule‑based inquiry dialog policies.

text: The discipline of computer science that seeks to construct machines capable of exhibiting behaviors regarded as intelligent by humans has long fascinated scholars. From antiquity’s fascination with artificial cognition to the modern era of computers and five decades of research in diverse programming paradigms, the vision of truly intelligent machines is approaching practical realization. Contemporary researchers have developed systems that emulate human reasoning, comprehend spoken language, defeat world‑class chess champions, and accomplish numerous tasks previously thought unattainable. Human proficiency in processing information is most evident in the use of natural language, where linguistic terms are employed to evaluate qualitative attributes. Such evaluations inevitably introduce uncertainty in the form of vagueness. Consequently, vague sets, vague judgments, and vague conclusions arise whenever a rational agent is involved and expresses interest in a particular subject. Vague‑set theory emerged as a response to the inherent imprecision of human language. The language of a rational agent is generated by vague events produced by reasoning and processed by the mind. Vague‑set theory offers an approximation of these imprecise groupings that is more suitable than classical set theory in contexts where natural language plays a central role; this framework was introduced by the American mathematicians Gau and Buehrer. In the present paper we demonstrate how the vagueness of linguistic variables can be addressed through vague‑set theory. The work is situated within the domain of eventology—the theory of random vague events—developed within probability theory to provide an event‑theoretic description of the dynamics of reasoning.

text: The Next Generation Air Transportation System is set to integrate sophisticated sensor technologies into flight decks, significantly expanding the scope of pilot responsibilities. The ALerting And Reasoning Management System (ALARMS) project, developed for NASA, addresses the critical challenge of managing aircraft sensor notifications efficiently. Continuous monitoring of all subsystems by the pilot is impractical, particularly given the inherent uncertainty regarding true hazard states despite sensor evidence, as well as the unpredictable outcomes and durations of corrective interventions. This research details the initial development of a system tailored for future alerting environments, categorizing 60 aircraft subsystems and 20 distinct hazards. We demonstrate the utility of Bayesian networks for inferring underlying hazard states from raw sensor data. Furthermore, we introduce a framework utilizing Time-Dependent Markov Processes (TMDPs) to facilitate collaborative hazard mitigation between the automated system and the pilot. The resulting automation policies adapt to varying hazard profiles and pilot states. The efficacy of this combined Bayesian and TMDP approach is evaluated through a use case involving multiple concurrent hazards, followed by an analysis of the generated alerting strategies.

text: Long Short‑Term Memory (LSTM) networks constitute a predominant recurrent architecture for modeling sequential data. Their design relies on gating mechanisms to regulate the flow of information—deciding, for instance, whether to retain or discard particular signals—yet conventional implementations based on soft (continuous) gates only approximate this principle. In this work we introduce a novel training paradigm that drives gate activations toward binary extremes (0 or 1). Consequently, the gates are predominantly either fully open or fully closed, reducing ambiguous intermediate states and enhancing interpretability of the information pathway. Extensive experiments demonstrate that: (1) despite an apparent reduction in model flexibility, performance does not deteriorate; in fact, the binary‑biased models achieve equal or superior results owing to improved generalization, and (2) gate outputs become largely insensitive to their inputs, enabling straightforward compression of LSTM units via techniques such as low‑rank and low‑precision approximations. Remarkably, the compressed variants often surpass the original uncompressed baselines.

text: Word reordering remains one of the most challenging components of statistical machine translation (SMT), profoundly influencing both translation quality and computational efficiency. Although a substantial body of research has been produced, the community’s interest in this issue persists, and no single technique has emerged as universally superior across different language pairs. Consequently, selecting the most appropriate method for a new translation task continues to rely heavily on empirical experimentation. To guide readers through this extensive and intricate field, we provide a thorough survey that treats word reordering both as a statistical modeling problem and as a linguistic phenomenon. The review details how reordering is represented in various string‑based and tree‑based SMT architectures, as well as in dedicated reordering tasks, offering systematic overviews of the literature on advanced reordering models. We then examine why certain approaches outperform others for specific language pairs. Beyond merely quantifying the amount of reordering, we argue that it is crucial to identify the particular types of reordering that arise in a given pair of languages. To this end, we perform a qualitative analysis of reordering phenomena across a diverse set of language pairs, drawing on an extensive repository of linguistic knowledge. Empirical findings from the SMT literature support the hypothesis that a small number of linguistic facts can reliably predict a language pair’s reordering behavior and help choose the SMT framework that best accommodates it.

text: A significant challenge in surveillance involves tracking multiple mobile agents within expansive, obstacle-dense environments characterized by frequent occlusions. This study introduces a formal framework based on Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) for the coordinated control of active camera networks tasked with high-resolution monitoring. The proposed methodology is designed to: (a) maintain a probabilistic belief state regarding target kinematics (position, heading, and velocity), facilitating tracking during periods of sensor occlusion; (b) synchronize camera operations to simultaneously refine state estimations and maximize the expected count of targets captured at a specified resolution; and (c) leverage the underlying structural properties of the surveillance task to ensure computational scalability, achieving linear complexity relative to the number of targets. Quantitative evaluations against existing multi-camera coordination strategies indicate that this approach delivers superior surveillance performance in real-time. Furthermore, the practical utility of the system is validated through implementation on physical AXIS 214 PTZ camera hardware.

text: BioSimplify is an open-source, Java-based software implementing a novel sentence simplification framework designed specifically to enhance automated information extraction and discourse analysis rather than human comprehension. Utilizing a "shot-gun" methodology, the tool generates multiple simplified iterations of a source sentence by integrating various permutations of its underlying components. Although optimized for biomedical text, such as PubMed abstracts, its utility was validated through protein-protein interaction (PPI) extraction tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that BioSimplify increased the PPI extraction F-score by approximately 7%, driven largely by a 20% improvement in recall. The software and associated evaluation corpora are available for download at https://biosimplify.sourceforge.net.

text: In this paper, we investigate the hybrid tractability of binary Quantified Constraint Satisfaction Problems (QCSPs). First, a basic tractable class of binary QCSPs is identified by using the broken-triangle property. In this class, the variable ordering for the broken-triangle property must be same as that in the prefix of the QCSP. Second, we break this restriction to allow that existentially quantified variables can be shifted within or out of their blocks, and thus identify some novel tractable classes by introducing the broken-angle property. Finally, we identify a more generalized tractable class, i.e., the min-of-max extendable class for QCSPs.

text: State-of-the-art named entity recognition (NER) systems are statistical machine learning models that exhibit strong generalization capabilities, i.e., they can identify unseen entities not present in the training data, by leveraging lexical and contextual information. However, such models can still err if their features bias toward an incorrect entity type. In this work, we leverage Wikipedia as an open knowledge base to enhance multilingual NER systems. A central element of our approach is the construction of high-accuracy, high-coverage multilingual Wikipedia entity-type mappings. These mappings are derived from weakly annotated data and can be extended to new languages without any human annotation or language-dependent knowledge. Based on these mappings, we develop several strategies to improve an NER system. We evaluate the effectiveness of the approaches through experiments on NER systems trained for six languages. The results show that the proposed approaches effectively improve the accuracy of such systems on unseen entities, particularly when deployed to a new domain or when trained with limited data (up to 18.3 F1-score improvement).

text: We present two new nonparametric statistical hypothesis tests. The first, called the relative dependency test, evaluates whether one source variable is significantly more dependent on a first target variable than on a second. Dependence is quantified by the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC). The second, called the relative similarity test, determines which of two samples from arbitrary distributions is significantly closer to a reference sample, with the relative similarity quantified by the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). To construct these tests, we use as test statistics the differences of HSIC statistics and of MMD statistics, respectively. The resulting tests are consistent and unbiased and exhibit favorable convergence properties. The effectiveness of the relative dependency test is demonstrated on several real-world problems: identifying language groups from a multilingual parallel corpus and showing that tumor location is more dependent on gene expression than on chromosome imbalance. We also illustrate the performance of the relative test of similarity over a broad selection of model comparison problems in deep generative models.

text: This paper presents a probabilistic framework that unifies Markov random fields of bounded treewidth with probabilistic context-free grammars. These models utilize case-factor diagrams (CFDs), a specialized representation for Boolean formulas. While sharing structural similarities with binary decision diagrams (BDDs), CFDs maintain conciseness for bounded treewidth circuits and can efficiently represent the space of parse trees for context-free grammars—capabilities that BDDs lack. Within this framework, a probabilistic model is defined by a CFD specifying a feasible set of Boolean assignments, with weights assigned to each variable. We provide an inside-outside algorithm for calculating the marginal probabilities of all Boolean variables simultaneously, alongside a Viterbi algorithm for identifying the minimum-cost assignment. Both procedures operate in linear time relative to the size of the CFD.

text: Coalition formation is a fundamental interaction that entails constructing coherent groups of distinct, autonomous agents in order to efficiently pursue their individual or shared objectives. A central challenge in multi-agent systems is determining which coalitions to form to achieve a given goal, which typically requires assigning a coalition value to each possible coalition to indicate the benefit of its formation. After these values are computed, agents must assemble a partition of the agent set into coalitions—each agent belonging to exactly one coalition—that maximizes the overall system outcome. The coalition structure generation problem is exceedingly difficult because the number of potential structures grows exponentially with the number of agents. Consequently, a variety of algorithms—ranging from dynamic programming and integer programming to stochastic search—have been proposed, yet all suffer from notable limitations in execution time, solution quality, or memory consumption. To address this, we develop an anytime algorithm for the coalition structure generation problem. The approach introduces a novel representation of the search space that partitions feasible solutions into subspaces, enabling computation of upper and lower bounds on the values of the best coalition structures within each subspace. These bounds are used to prune subspaces that cannot contain the optimal solution. The remaining subspaces are explored with a branch-and-bound strategy, efficiently traversing them without exhaustively enumerating all solutions within the examined regions. We prove that the algorithm enumerates all coalition structures efficiently by automatically discarding redundant and invalid solutions. To assess the method, we also introduce a new input distribution designed to yield more reliable benchmarks than those previously used in the literature. Under this distribution, for 27 agents our algorithm finds optimal solutions in only 0.175% of the time required by the fastest algorithm reported in the literature. The algorithm is anytime: if interrupted before its usual termination, it still delivers a solution with a provable bound relative to the optimum. Moreover, the guarantees on solution quality are substantially better than those of prior state-of-the-art approaches. For example, on a worst-case distribution with 25 agents, the method achieves a solution that is 90% efficient in roughly 10% of the time required to obtain the optimum.

text: Statistical null hypotheses are standard in the hard sciences but have seen limited use in theoretical linguistics. Here the null hypothesis that a low frequency of syntactic dependency crossings arises from an arbitrary word order is rejected. It is shown that accepting such a null would require star-shaped dependency structures, which are unrealistic and overly restrictive. The hypothesis of limited cognitive resources in the human brain is reevaluated. Stronger null hypotheses that incorporate actual dependency lengths when assessing the likelihood of crossings are introduced. These hypotheses suggest that crossings become less likely as dependency lengths shorten. A hypothesis based on pressure to reduce dependency lengths is more parsimonious than a principle of crossing minimization or a grammatical ban that is completely dissociated from the general, non-linguistic principle of economy.

text: In this work, we establish theoretical connections between Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) and Bayesian Networks (BNs). We prove that every SPN can be transformed into a BN in time and space linear in the size of the network. The central idea is to employ Algebraic Decision Diagrams (ADDs) to compactly encode the local conditional probability distributions at each BN node by exploiting context-specific independence (CSI). The resulting BN exhibits a simple directed bipartite structure. We show that applying the Variable Elimination (VE) algorithm to the ADD-based BN allows us to recover the original SPN, with the SPN interpretable as a history of VE inference or as a cache of intermediate results. To clarify the proof, we introduce the notion of a normal SPN and provide a theoretical analysis of its consistency and decomposability properties. We conclude with a discussion of the implications and establish a connection between the depth of an SPN and a lower bound on the tree-width of its corresponding BN.

text: Nicod's criterion posits that observing a black raven provides evidence for the hypothesis H that all ravens are black. We show that Solomonoff induction does not conform to Nicod's criterion: there exist time steps in which observing black ravens reduces the posterior probability of H. Moreover, for any computable infinite string compatible with H, the belief in H decreases infinitely often when using the unnormalized Solomonoff prior, whereas this occurs only finitely often when using the normalized Solomonoff prior. We argue that the fault lies not with Solomonoff induction itself, but with Nicod's criterion, which should be abandoned.

Let's craft: "The syntactic topic model (STM) is a Bayesian nonparametric framework that learns latent word distributions—topics—that are coherent both semantically and syntactically. It operates on dependency‑parsed corpora, treating sentences as grouped within documents. Simultaneously, every node in the dependency parse tree is associated with a distribution over the topics of its children, mirroring latent‑state syntax models and guaranteeing syntactic consistency. We develop a fast variational inference procedure for the posterior. Experiments on synthetic data and manually parsed corpora demonstrate that the STM outperforms models that rely solely on syntax or solely on topics in predictive performance."

To construct the semantic models, we analyze the descriptions to extract syntactic structure and lexical categories. The resulting meanings are grounded through soft‑constraint representations. The system’s generated descriptions incorporate contextual information to reduce ambiguity, achieving a correct‑guess rate of 72 %.

text: Punctuation serves as a reliable marker of syntactic organization, and parsers developed on conventionally punctuated text typically depend substantially on this feature. Yet this dependence is problematic, as human language comprehension does not utilize punctuation to the same degree, and informal writing frequently omits it altogether. Additionally, punctuation is sometimes employed in non-standard ways for stylistic emphasis, creative expression, or simply through error. This work demonstrates that (a) dependency parsers exhibit vulnerability to both the removal of punctuation and its unconventional application; (b) neural-based parsers display greater susceptibility than traditional parsing approaches; (c) neural parsers trained on unpunctuated text achieve superior performance compared to standard pre-trained parsers in all cases involving non-standard punctuation usage. The primary analysis employs artificially modified datasets to isolate punctuation effects while minimizing confounding variables, supplemented by evaluation on authentic out-of-domain text.

text: Markov Networks represent a fundamental tool in computer vision and machine learning applications. A particularly important category within this framework is Associative Markov Networks, which have demonstrated utility across numerous practical domains. For this network class, efficient computation of approximate optimal solutions is achievable through graph cut-based optimization techniques, such as alpha-expansion algorithms. An extension of this approach, termed the associative hierarchical network, has recently emerged as a natural extension to accommodate higher-order cliques beyond pairwise interactions. This generalized model proves particularly valuable for addressing object class segmentation tasks in computer vision. This work presents the associative hierarchical network formulation and introduces a computationally tractable graph cut-based inference algorithm. The proposed approach scales effectively to problems involving hundreds of thousands of variables with higher-order potentials spanning tens of thousands of variables per clique, a scale at which conventional linear programming approaches become impractical. We establish a 4-approximation bound for the general associative hierarchical network across arbitrary clique sizes, contributing to the limited body of existing approximation guarantees for Markov Network inference with higher-order cliques.

text: Collaborative datasets comprise ratings that connect two separate categories of entities: users and items. Previous research on such data has predominantly concentrated on filtering techniques aimed at estimating missing ratings for user-item combinations. This work addresses an alternative challenge: the visual representation of collaborative data. Our objective is to position both users and items as points within a shared Euclidean space, such that users are located proximate to items they have rated or would likely rate favorably, while maintaining distance from items they would rate unfavorably. We formulate this embedding problem as a continuous-valued nonlinear Bayesian network and apply Markov chain Monte Carlo and expectation maximization algorithms to derive the embedding solution. We introduce an evaluation metric for assessing visualization quality and benchmark our approach against local linear embedding and Eigentaste using three empirical datasets.

These findings provide knowledge engineers with a systematic method for identifying high-impact parameters and offer a theoretical foundation for interpreting prior empirical observations regarding the robustness of probabilistic networks.

text: Dictionary-based Cross-language Information Retrieval (CLIR) encounters significant obstacles, including polysemy in translation, absent vocabulary items in bilingual lexicons, and incomplete translation coverage. These challenges are particularly acute for agglutinative languages lacking robust stemming algorithms, where the absence of morphological variants in bilingual dictionaries substantially diminishes retrieval effectiveness. To address these limitations, this work presents a probabilistic framework for resolving translation ambiguity and generating plausible morphological variants of candidate terms. We introduce the Minimum Edit Support Candidates (MESC) technique, which leverages monolingual corpora alongside bilingual lexicons to convert queries from the source language into the target language of the document collection. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing dictionary-based methods in English-Persian CLIR tasks.

text: Touch, as the first sensory modality to emerge during human development, serves as a fundamental component in our interactions with the physical world. Many object manipulation tasks depend on integrating tactile information to successfully execute desired actions, yet creating effective haptic feedback mechanisms remains a significant challenge. This study addresses manipulation tasks where tactile sensor data must inform adjustments to predetermined motion plans. To handle incomplete sensory information, we propose a framework that formulates the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process and learns an effective representation of haptic signals that functions as the state variable within this POMDP formulation. The approach employs deep recurrent neural networks as the underlying model architecture and applies variational Bayesian inference to refine the approximate posterior distribution. We extend deep Q-learning techniques to enable optimal action selection at each state without requiring access to a simulation environment. The proposed method is evaluated on a PR2 robotic platform across several instantiations of a rotary knob manipulation task that terminates upon auditory and tactile confirmation.
